stories.title: Nvidia Moves to Buy the Library of Open AI
stories.story:
Nvidia reportedly agreed to acquire Hugging Face — the GitHub of artificial intelligence — for roughly $12.9 billion, a deal that would be the chipmaker's largest purchase ever and one of the most structurally significant moves in the short history of the AI industry.

Hugging Face is not a household name, but it is the plumbing beneath an enormous share of AI development. Founded in 2016, it is where researchers publish models, developers download and fine-tune them, and teams collaborate on datasets. Closing it off, or merely reorienting it, would reshape who can build AI and on what terms.

The logic from Nvidia's side is almost elegant in its ruthlessness. OpenAI, Anthropic, and other closed-source labs have been racing to design their own inference chips — explicitly to reduce dependence on Nvidia's hardware. Nvidia's counter-move: own the open-source ecosystem those same labs compete against. The more open models flourish, the more GPU-hours they consume. As one internal Nvidia view holds, a wealth of open models helps uphold the company's dominance in AI hardware, because those models directly counter the closed-source developers trying to build rival chips.

The price is also a statement. Hugging Face's annualized revenue climbed from roughly $100 million to $150 million in just two months this year — and Nvidia appears willing to pay close to 86 times that revenue. That multiple only makes sense if you treat the acquisition as buying leverage over the entire open-source AI stack, not a software business.

As of today, no signed contract exists. But Nvidia's silence — a company known for quickly rebutting inaccurate reports — is itself telling.
stories.hook: Nvidia isn't just selling shovels in the gold rush anymore — it's buying the map room.

stories.title: Stripe and Advent Walk Away from PayPal, Leaving a Giant Stranded
stories.story:
The numbers tell a brutal story. In 2021, PayPal was worth roughly $360 billion — a pandemic-era colossus processing the world's shift to digital commerce. This morning, after Stripe and private equity firm Advent International abandoned their pursuit of the company, PayPal shares slumped 16% in premarket trading, leaving it valued at barely $52 billion. That is not a correction. It is a verdict.

The deal that fell apart would have been one of the largest leveraged buyouts in history. Earlier this summer, the Stripe-Advent consortium bid $60.50 per share — implying a total value of more than $53 billion — a 28% premium over where PayPal was then trading. PayPal's board rejected the offer as inadequate and never formally responded. The suitors, apparently unwilling to sweeten the bid further into a company whose trajectory remains uncertain, have now walked away entirely.

The strategic logic of the deal had been compelling. A merger would have let Stripe reduce its dependence on Visa and Mastercard by absorbing PayPal's proprietary rails, while folding in Venmo's 90-million-user consumer wallet and PayPal's growing crypto infrastructure. For PayPal, Stripe's $159 billion valuation and engineering culture might have provided the transformation its board has failed to execute alone — ousting one CEO and installing HP's Enrique Lores in March in a sign of mounting desperation.

What the collapse reveals is a classic standoff between a seller anchored to past glory and a buyer disciplined about price. PayPal's board, staring at a company still 85% below its peak, concluded that $53 billion was an insult. Stripe and Advent concluded that paying more for a turnaround that might not come was a worse mistake. Neither side blinked, and now PayPal faces its restructuring alone — in a payments market where Apple Pay and Google Pay are gaining ground every quarter.
stories.hook: PayPal's board turned down a $53 billion offer because they thought it was too low — and now they get to find out if they were right.

stories.title: Anthropic Eyes the Largest IPO in History This October
stories.story:
Five years ago, Anthropic was a splinter group of ex-OpenAI researchers with a safety thesis and no product. Today, investors expect it to go public in October at a valuation of at least $2 trillion — which would make it the largest stock-market debut in history, surpassing SpaceX's $1.77 trillion June offering.

The arithmetic behind that number is almost hallucinatory. Anthropic reached a $965 billion valuation in May after a $65 billion Series H round. Just eight months before that, in September 2025, the company was worth $183 billion. A $2 trillion IPO print would represent an eleven-fold increase in thirteen months. Half a dozen backers told the Financial Times they expect annualized revenue to land between $100 billion and $120 billion before year-end — a figure that would represent more than tenfold growth from the $47 billion annualized run rate reported in May.

The mechanism driving this is enterprise adoption. Anthropic has gained ground against OpenAI and Google precisely by selling its models directly to business customers at scale, rather than chasing consumer eyeballs. Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan are reportedly running the book.

But the bull case has real fracture lines. Anthropic's top model is priced more than 2.5 times higher than OpenAI's flagship, while Chinese open-weight alternatives can be accessed at a fraction of the cost. Revenue growth reportedly slowed in June after the Commerce Department imposed temporary export controls on its best models. And unlike traditional software, where a sale is nearly pure margin, frontier AI burns compute at enormous scale — raising genuine questions about whether free cash flow can ever justify the valuation.

The $2 trillion figure is investor speculation, not a company-issued target; senior Anthropic executives have not settled on a number even in private. What the IPO will actually test is whether the market believes foundation model companies are permanent infrastructure — or extraordinarily expensive science projects.
stories.hook: The question isn't whether Anthropic is worth two trillion dollars — it's whether 'worth' means anything at all when revenue multiples are measured in decades.
